title: A Parish for the Autopsy
premise: Paloma Kavanagh, archivist of St. Aldhelm's Cathedral, has a private habit of solving the deaths the police file away as accidents. When a drowned man is found wearing clothes stolen from Paloma's own closet, they become both suspect and investigator, forced to reopen a thirty-year-old scandal involving the cathedral's locked crypt and a trial that never quite explained itself. As Paloma traces alibis woven by the cathedral's old guard — including their own late mentor — they discover the found family that raised them was built to bury a crime. The killer is the cathedral's beloved canon, who murdered to keep the crypt's secret sealed; in the final courtroom reckoning, Paloma chooses truth over belonging, unlocking the crypt and finding a new family among those willing to face what's inside.
about_author: Ivo Marchetti is the pen name of a former parish records clerk from Trieste who spent a decade cataloguing deaths in church registries before turning to fiction. They write mysteries about institutions, archives, and the quiet violence of respectability.

chapters.title: The Locked Crypt
chapters.summary: Paloma Kavanagh's POV. Establishes daily life among the cathedral archives: ledgers, dust, the iron door of the crypt no one holds a key to. A brief flashback shows how Paloma quietly solved three 'accidental' deaths. Emotional beat: solitary competence masking loneliness.

chapters.title: A Body in Borrowed Clothes
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A drowned man is pulled from the millrace wearing Paloma's own stolen coat and scarf. Police treat Paloma as witness, then person of interest. Emotional beat: violation — someone has worn their life like a costume.

chapters.title: Detective Okafor
chapters.summary: Detective Adaeze Okafor's POV. She knows Paloma's unofficial reputation from the earlier cases and grudgingly offers an uneasy alliance: help me, stay free. Emotional beat: wary mutual recognition between two people who distrust institutions.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Alibis
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The victim is identified as Tomas Reyes, once a stonemason's apprentice tied to a 1990s scandal when the crypt was sealed after a girl's death. Every living witness has an airtight alibi — too airtight. Emotional beat: dread beneath routine.

chapters.title: The Canon's Kindness
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Canon Ambrose Ellery, Paloma's mentor and surrogate father figure, offers comfort and quiet warnings about digging into old grief. His warmth reads as love; his phrasing reads as instruction. Emotional beat: comfort with a cold current under it.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Doesn't Say
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, with archive documents interleaved. A gap in the restoration ledger covers exactly the weeks before the girl's death. Someone paid for work never recorded. Emotional beat: the thrill of the hunt sharpening into fear.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Recanted
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. The original trial's star witness, now dying of cancer, admits she lied about seeing the mason's apprentice near the crypt — she was paid by a man whose face she never saw, only his voice at evensong. Emotional beat: guilt finally surfacing.

chapters.title: Found Family
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Flashbacks woven through present scenes: how Ellery took in orphaned teenage Paloma, gave them the archive, gave them belonging. Now every memory must be re-read for evidence. Emotional beat: grief for a childhood being dismantled.

chapters.title: Second Theft
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Another item vanishes from Paloma's flat — this time a photograph of Paloma and Ellery at the crypt door. The killer is staging intimacy, framing Paloma deliberately. Emotional beat: hunted.

chapters.title: The Stonemason's Daughter
chapters.summary: New character POV: Marisol Reyes, the dead man's sister, arrives demanding answers. She reveals Tomas came back to town because he'd received letters threatening to reveal what he saw in the crypt in 1994. Emotional beat: shared loss forging an alliance.

chapters.title: Evensong Voices
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Chasing the recanting witness's clue, Okafor collects voice recordings of clergy from old services. Three men sang evensong that year; two are dead of 'accidents.' Emotional beat: pattern recognition turning to horror.

chapters.title: Accident Number Four
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The dying witness is found dead hours before a formal interview — a fall down her own stairs, ruled accidental. Paloma realizes the killer is erasing the past faster than they can excavate it. Emotional beat: fury and futility.

chapters.title: The Trial Begins
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Pretrial hearing opens on Paloma as suspect; the prosecution weaves the stolen clothes, the missing photograph, and Paloma's history of 'meddling' into a portrait of obsession. Emotional beat: public unmasking, the belonging they built now weaponized against them.

chapters.title: Alibi Woven Thirty Years Ago
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Cross-referencing parish rotas, she finds all four 'accidents' occurred on nights one specific cleric claimed to be alone in the tower — unverifiable, always. But the rotas were signed by a young archivist: Ellery himself. Emotional beat: the trap closing on the wrong person.

chapters.title: What Tomas Saw
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV, with Tomas's recovered letter. In 1994, Tomas repaired the crypt wall and saw the girl alive after her supposed death — hidden, not killed, by someone protecting her from something worse. The sealing wasn't concealment of murder but of a life. Emotional beat: the mystery inverting.

chapters.title: The Girl in the Crypt
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Records search reveals the girl survived, was smuggled out, and lives under another name — and that Ellery funded her escape, then spent thirty years killing anyone who might expose the conspiracy that made it necessary. Emotional beat: moral vertigo.

chapters.title: Confession at the Rail
chapters.summary: Ellery's POV, intimate and chilling. He explains his arithmetic: four deaths weighed against a girl's life and the cathedral's soul. He believes he is owed gratitude, especially from Paloma. Emotional beat: love and menace indistinguishable.

chapters.title: The Choice
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Ellery offers a deal: destroy the evidence, keep the family, let the dead stay dead. Paloma, facing conviction, must choose between the only belonging they've ever had and the truth. Emotional beat: the book's thematic crux — power corrupting even love.

chapters.title: Unlocking the Door
chapters.summary: Climax. Paloma's POV. Paloma leads Okafor and Marisol to the crypt with the key Ellery unknowingly surrendered years ago, recorded confession running. Ellery confronts them inside the dark; a tense standoff ends with his arrest as dawn enters through the opened door. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into release.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At trial, Paloma testifies, dismantling the frame piece by piece and placing Ellery at every death. The stolen-clothes trick unravels: CCTV of the second theft shows Ellery's curate. Emotional beat: reclaiming one's own narrative in public.

chapters.title: Verdict
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Guilty on four counts. Ellery, led away, asks Paloma if it was worth losing everything; Paloma answers that he taught them what archives are for — so nothing stays buried that shouldn't. Emotional beat: justice without triumphalism.

chapters.title: A Parish Rebuilt
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, epilogue. Months later: the crypt open as a memorial, the surviving girl reunited with Marisol, Okafor sharing case files over coffee, Paloma no longer solving alone. Belonging rebuilt on truth instead of silence. Emotional beat: found family, honestly founded.
